summary: This unit teaches you to give customers polite, honest and reliable service, whether you are welding a gate, wiring a house or answering the workshop phone. You will learn who your customers are, how to present yourself, how to communicate and find out what customers need, how to work in their homes and businesses, how to serve customers with different needs, and how to handle complaints, follow up and keep good records.

blocks.p: Good work is only half of a good job. The customer also remembers whether you arrived when you said, whether you listened, whether you explained things in words they understood, whether you kept their home clean and safe, and how you dealt with a problem. That is **customer service**, and in a trade business it decides whether the customer comes back, pays on time and tells others about you.

**Who it is for:** this is a general unit in several Level 2 programmes, including Welding and Electrical Installation, so the examples come from fabrication shops, electrical contractors, customers' homes and businesses, and villas and guest houses. The skills are the same whatever your trade.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means at work
rows: Understand customers and quality service
Know who your customers are (outside and inside the business), what they expect, and why good service matters.
Present yourself professionally
Look, speak and behave in a way that makes customers trust you from the first moment.
Communicate well
Listen actively, ask the right questions, use plain words and positive body language, and handle phone calls, messages and notes properly.
Find out and meet customer needs
Learn exactly what the customer wants, explain the choices, agree the work, price and date, and keep your promises.
Work in customers' homes and businesses
Arrive on time, protect their property, keep their family safe, keep them informed, clean up and hand over properly.
Serve customers with different needs
Treat every customer with equal respect, and adapt your help for older people, people with disabilities and visitors.
Handle complaints and difficult situations
Listen, apologise, solve or refer, record and follow up; stay calm with angry customers and keep yourself safe.
Follow up, keep records and work as a team
Check customers are satisfied, collect feedback, keep accurate and private records, and pass information on.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on customers, presentation, communication, finding needs, phone calls, working on site, different needs, complaints, business rules, follow-up and teamwork.
A **written paper** with short answers (exact terms such as warranty, body language, confidentiality, quotation, invoice, ETA, jargon, complaints log) and longer answers in full sentences.
**Practical role plays**: welcoming a customer, finding out their needs and filling in a job request form; and handling a complaint, recording it and making a follow-up call.

blocks.note: In role plays the assessor watches what you do as much as what you say: your greeting, your face and posture, whether you let the customer finish, whether you read details back, and whether you agree a clear next step.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A **customer** is anyone who receives a product or a service from you, whether they pay or not.

head: Kind of customer
Who they are
Examples
rows: External customers
People outside the business who buy from it or use its service
A home owner who wants a gate; a shop owner who needs more sockets; a villa manager who needs a handrail repaired; a guest at the villa
Internal customers
People inside the business who need **your** work to do **their** job
The welder who needs the measurements you took; the painter waiting for your finished frame; the office clerk who needs your job sheet to invoice the customer

blocks.p: Serve internal customers as well as external ones. If the measurements are wrong or the job sheet is late, the external customer gets a poor job in the end.

head: Customers expect
What it means in practice
rows: Reliability
You do what you said, when you said: arrive on time, finish by the agreed date, at the agreed price
Responsiveness
Calls and messages answered promptly; problems dealt with quickly
Competence and honesty
Safe, neat, correct work; honest advice, even when the honest answer earns you less
Courtesy and respect
A greeting, polite words, patience, and respect for their home, time and privacy
Understanding
You listen, take their situation into account and explain things clearly
A tidy, professional look
Clean work clothes, ID, tidy tools and vehicle, clear paperwork

blocks.p: **Quality customer service** means meeting these expectations every time, from the first phone call to the follow-up after the job. Many businesses write down the level of service they promise every customer, such as "we return every call within one working day". These **service standards** (sometimes a **customer charter**) tell staff what to aim for.

ul: **Repeat customers** come back again and again: most trade work comes from people who have used you before.
**Word of mouth**: happy customers tell family, friends and neighbours, and online reviews spread further still.
**Customer satisfaction** brings fewer complaints, faster payment and less time spent putting things right.
The business's **good name** grows, and so does the work, which means steadier jobs and pay for its staff.
Poor service loses customers quietly: many never complain, they simply go elsewhere and tell others why.

blocks.p: Going the extra mile means doing something helpful that the customer did not expect, **within the business's rules**: pointing out a loose hinge or a damaged cable you noticed and offering to quote for it, showing how to look after the new gate, or sweeping the yard where you worked. It does **not** mean doing extra work and adding it to the bill without asking.
Customers decide very quickly whether to trust you, often before you have said much. That **first impression** is hard to change. It comes from how you look, how you greet them and how you behave.

head: Area
Do
Do not
rows: Appearance
Clean work clothes or uniform; your **ID badge** (identification) where it can be seen; safety boots; neat hair
Turn up in torn or dirty clothes, or in party clothes and jewellery that are unsafe on a job
Punctuality
Arrive on time; if you will be late, call before the agreed time with a new **ETA** (estimated time of arrival)
Arrive late without a word, or not come at all
Greeting
Greet the customer first, politely, with your name and the business's name, and ask how you can help
Wait for them to speak, or carry on a phone call while they stand there
Attitude
Polite, helpful, honest and positive; patient with questions
Rude, rushed, careless with details, or "that's not my job"
Behaviour
Keep your phone for work; speak politely to co-workers in front of customers
Smoke, swear, play loud music, gossip about other customers, or argue with co-workers in front of them
Tools and vehicle
Tidy and in good order
A dirty van full of rubbish, or tools left lying about

blocks.note: In Jamaica a greeting matters: "Good morning" or "Good afternoon" before anything else is basic good manners, and many older customers expect to be called Miss, Mrs or Mr with their surname, not by their first name, unless they invite it.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.h: A customer arrives while you are busy

ul: If you are serving one customer and another arrives, smile, greet the new customer and say you will be with them shortly. Then finish with the first customer.
If you are on the phone, look up, smile and signal that you have seen them; end the call politely as soon as you can.
Never leave the first customer to serve the second, and never ignore anyone who is waiting.

blocks.p: A **business card** is a small printed card with your name, the business's name and a phone number. Give one to new customers, so they know who you are and how to reach the business.
**Active listening** means giving the customer your full attention and checking that you have understood them. It is the most important customer-service skill.

flow: Stop what you are doing, face the customer and make eye contact
Let them finish; do not interrupt or jump to a solution
Show you are listening: nod, and say "I see" or "Yes"
Make short notes of the key facts: sizes, places, dates, budget
Ask questions to fill the gaps
Repeat the main points back in your own words to check you have them right: "So you'd like ... is that right?"

head: Kind of question
What it does
Examples
rows: Open
Gets the customer talking and gives you information; cannot be answered with yes or no
"What will the grill be used for?" "Which rooms need extra sockets?" "How do you use the back door?"
Closed
Confirms one detail; answered with yes, no or a short fact
"Is the opening 900 mm wide?" "Would you like it painted black?" "Is Tuesday good for the visit?"
Probing
Digs deeper into something the customer said
"When exactly do the lights go off: all the time, or when the kettle is on?"

blocks.p: Use **open** questions to explore what the customer wants, then **closed** questions to confirm the details. When a customer reports a fault ("my lights keep going off"), ask questions to find out when and where it happens before you suggest a cause or a cure.
**Jargon** is trade or technical words that most customers do not understand. Use plain words, or explain the trade word the first time you use it.

head: Trade word
Plain words for a customer
rows: RCD or RCBO
The safety trip switch that cuts the power if current leaks to earth
MCB
The circuit breaker that switches off a circuit if it is overloaded
Galvanised
Coated with zinc to stop rust
Fillet weld
The weld along the corner where two pieces meet
Square tube, 25 mm
Hollow square steel bar, about one inch across
Primer
The first coat of paint that stops rust and helps the top coat stick

ul: Speak clearly, at a steady pace, in a friendly tone. Customers hear a smile, even on the phone.

Jamaican Creole is a natural part of everyday talk, but switch to clear Standard English with customers who do not use it, with visitors from abroad, and in formal situations such as quotations and complaints.
Avoid slang and swearing, and never talk down to a customer.

blocks.p: **Body language** (non-verbal communication) is what your face, eyes, hands and posture say without words. Customers believe it more than your words.

head: Shows interest and respect
Shows you do not care
rows: Facing the customer, with eye contact
Turning away to look at your work or your phone
Nodding and a friendly face
Rolling your eyes, sighing or frowning
Open, relaxed posture; hands visible
Arms folded, hands in pockets, leaning on the wall
A comfortable distance, at the customer's level
Standing too close, or talking down from above

flow: Answer promptly, within a few rings
Greet the caller, give the business's name and your name, and ask how you can help: "Good morning, [business], Kimberley speaking. How can I help you?"
Listen and make notes; answer only what you know, and never guess
To put a caller on hold, ask first, say why and roughly how long, and come back to them within that time
If the person they want is not there, offer to take a message
Read the message and number back to check them, say who will call back and when, and thank them
Pass the message on at once, and check later that it was dealt with

head: A phone message must include
Why
rows: Who it is for
So it reaches the right person
The caller's name (spelt correctly) and phone number
So they can be called back
What it is about, and how urgent it is
So the right action is taken in time
The date and time of the call
So everyone knows how long the caller has waited
Your name
So anyone with a question knows whom to ask

ul: When you leave a **voicemail** for a customer, say your name and the business, why you are calling, and your number slowly, twice. Keep it short.
If a customer asks something you do not know, such as when their gate will be ready, do not guess. Say you will check, and give a time you will call back by, then keep to it.
Reply to customers' messages and emails as soon as you can in working hours, even if only to say when you will answer fully.
Write politely and clearly, with a greeting, correct spelling, and no slang, ALL CAPITALS or rows of emojis.
Put prices, dates and agreements in writing, so both sides have a record.
Use the business's phone or account for customers, as your employer's rules say.

sections.title: Finding out and meeting customer needs

flow: Greet the customer and give your name
Let them explain in their own words; listen without interrupting
Ask open questions to explore, then closed questions to confirm sizes, colours, the address and the date they need it by
Ask about their budget, and explain the choices in plain words, with the good and weak points and the price of each
Write the details on the **job request** (enquiry) form
Read the main points back to check them
Agree the next step, such as a site visit to measure, and say when they will hear from you

blocks.p: Customers often want two things that pull against each other, such as a cheap grill that will also keep out thieves. Do not just sell the cheapest or the dearest. Explain the options honestly (for example, thinner bar is cheaper but easier to cut through; heavier bar and better fixings cost more but are much stronger), show photos or samples of past work, and let the customer decide with the facts in front of them.
Before work starts, agree **what will be done, the price and the finish date**, so that both sides know what to expect and there are no arguments later. Put it in writing.

head: Document
What it is
What it shows
rows: Quotation (quote)
A fixed price for the work, given before the job is agreed
The work and materials, the price (and whether GCT is included), how long the price is valid, the expected finish time, any deposit, and the terms
Job sheet or work order
The instruction to the team to do the job
The customer, address, work, materials, and who does it
Invoice (bill)
Asks the customer to pay for work done
The work done, the amount due, GCT where it applies, and how and when to pay
Receipt
Proof that the customer has paid
The amount paid, the date, and what it was for
Warranty (guarantee)
A written promise that faulty work or parts will be put right free for a set time
What is covered, for how long, and what is not covered

ul: Do what you said you would do, when you said you would. That is how customers learn to trust you and the business.
Promise only what you can deliver. A realistic date kept is better than an early date missed.
If something will be late (materials delayed, rain, a sick co-worker), **tell the customer before the deadline**, say sorry, explain briefly, and give a new date.
If you made a mistake, such as giving the wrong collection date, contact the customer quickly, apologise and put it right. Never cover it up or blame someone else.

blocks.h: When a customer asks for something unsafe

blocks.p: Sometimes a customer asks for something that is unsafe or against the rules: to remove the safety trip switch because it keeps tripping, to add sockets to a circuit that is already overloaded, to weld a gate without proper hinges or fixings, or to skip a test to save money. The customer is not always right when safety is at stake. Explain the danger in plain words, offer the safe way (with its price), and if they still insist, refuse politely and tell your supervisor. Never do unsafe work to please a customer.

blocks.note: New electrical installations in Jamaica must be inspected and certified before the power company will connect them, and safety devices are there by law and for good reason. A worker who removes or bypasses one puts lives at risk and is responsible for what follows.
blocks.label: Jamaica

sections.title: Working at the customer's home or business

ul: Confirm the day and time with the customer the day before.
Check you have the right materials, tools, PPE and paperwork, so you do not need to leave halfway.
If you are running late, call before the agreed time, apologise and give a new ETA.
Introduce yourself, show your ID, and explain what you will do today and how long it will take.
Ask where to park, where to work, where to put tools and materials, and where you may plug in or get water.
Ask permission before moving furniture or anything else, and ask the customer to put away valuables or fragile items near the work.
Ask about pets: keep gates and doors closed behind you, and ask the owner to secure dogs while you work.

head: Do
Why
rows: Lay **dust sheets** over floors, furniture and counters; protect tiles from sparks and spatter
The customer's property must be left as you found it
Tell the customer **before** the power or water goes off, for how long, and when it will be back; agree a time that suits them where you can
They can plan: save computer work, stop cooking, keep the freezer shut, warn their own customers
Warn them about noise, fumes and sparks from grinding, welding or painting
They can close windows, move washing and keep people away
Put up screens, barriers and signs; keep children and pets away from the work
Arc light, sparks, cables and open holes are dangerous to the family
Keep tools, cables and offcuts tidy and out of walkways
No one trips, and the place looks cared for
Do not use the customer's things (phone, tools, bathroom, food) without asking
It is their home or business
Keep private matters private
What you see and hear in a customer's home stays there

blocks.note: If you are welding at a house and children or neighbours gather to watch, stop, put up screens, and ask an adult to keep them back. Arc light burns the eyes of anyone who can see it, and sunglasses or clear glasses do not protect them.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Test the work: the gate swings and locks, the lights and sockets work, the RCD trips when tested
Clean up fully: offcuts, stubs, wire clippings, dust and spatter; take your rubbish away unless agreed otherwise
Show the customer the finished work and explain it in plain words
Explain how to use and look after it: oiling hinges, touching up paint, resetting a trip switch and what to do if it keeps tripping
Give the paperwork: invoice, certificate or warranty, and your business card
Ask whether they are happy, and deal with any small point there and then
Thank them for their business

blocks.p: Every customer deserves the **same respect**, whatever their age, sex, race, religion, disability, accent, appearance or how much money they seem to have. Equal respect does not mean identical treatment: it means adapting the way you help so that each person gets the same good service.

head: Customer
How you can help
rows: An older customer
Be patient and give them time to decide
Speak clearly and face them
Offer a seat if they have to wait or talk for a while
Write down the key points: price, date, your name and number
A customer who is hard of hearing or deaf
Face them in good light so they can see your lips; do not cover your mouth
Speak clearly at a normal pace; do not shout
Write things down, or use gestures and pictures
Check they have understood
A customer with poor sight
Say who you are as you approach
Read out important details
Offer large print, or to explain papers aloud
A wheelchair user or someone with a walking aid
Speak to them at their level: come round a high counter, or sit
Keep the way in clear
Do not lean on or move the wheelchair without asking
A person with a disability and a companion
Speak to the customer directly, not to the companion, and ask how you can help instead of guessing
A visitor from abroad, or someone with little English
Speak a little slower, in simple Standard English, without slang, Creole or jargon
Use drawings, photos and numbers written down
A translation app on a phone can help
Check understanding without making them feel foolish
A customer who is worried or upset
Listen first, show you understand, and explain clearly what will happen next
A customer in a hurry
Get to the point, confirm the key details quickly, and agree when you will follow up

blocks.note: In tourist areas, villa and guest-house work often brings you into contact with visitors from many countries. They judge the whole island by the people they meet. Courtesy, patience and honesty from every worker matter.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A complaint is a chance, not an attack. It shows what needs fixing, and a complaint handled well often turns an unhappy customer into a loyal one. Most unhappy customers never complain; they just go elsewhere. **Welcome** complaints.

flow: **Listen** to the whole complaint without interrupting, arguing or making excuses; stay calm and take notes
**Apologise** that they have had a problem, and thank them for telling you (you can say sorry before you know whose fault it is)
Ask questions to find out exactly what is wrong; look at the work if you can
**Solve**: offer a fair solution within the business's rules and agree a time, or pass it to your supervisor and tell the customer when they will hear back
**Thank** the customer, and **record** the complaint and the action in the complaints log
**Follow up** once it is fixed, to check the customer is now happy

head: Do
Do not
rows: Show you understand: "I can see why that is upsetting."
Say "That's not my fault" or blame the supplier, the weather or a co-worker
Keep to facts and solutions
Argue about who is right
Promise only what you can deliver
Make promises to calm them down that cannot be kept
Bring in your supervisor when the matter is beyond you
Refuse to help, or leave the customer waiting with no answer

blocks.h: What you may decide, and what you refer

blocks.p: Every business has rules on prices, discounts, refunds, warranties, deposits and repairs. Know them, so that you give customers correct and fair answers and every customer is treated the same. When a customer asks for something outside your authority, such as a big discount or a refund, do not say yes and do not flatly refuse. Say honestly that you cannot approve it yourself, that you will ask your supervisor, and when they will hear back.

head: Record
Example
rows: Date and time; who took the complaint
12 March, 10:15 a.m., taken by Kevin
Customer's name, address and phone number
As on the job sheet
The job, and what the complaint is
Burglar bars fitted 4 March rattle in the wind; paint drips on tiles
What was agreed, who will do it, and by when
Return Friday to add fixings and clean tiles; Kevin and the fitter
The outcome and the follow-up
Fixed Friday; customer called Tuesday and is satisfied

ul: Stay calm and do not take it personally: the customer is usually angry about the problem, not about you.
Let them speak. Keep your voice low and steady, your body language open, and a safe distance between you.
Show you understand, then move to the facts and what can be done.
Never shout back, argue, or walk away leaving them alone in the office.

blocks.note: If a customer becomes threatening or violent, your safety comes first. Do not argue or threaten back. Move to a safe place, get your supervisor or co-workers, and if needed call the police (119 in Jamaica). Afterwards, report and record what happened.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Situation
What to do
rows: A customer asks a neighbour's or another customer's business: what work you did, or what it cost
Politely say you cannot share another customer's details. **Confidentiality** means keeping customers' private information secret.
A customer offers you cash "for yourself" to do the job cheaper, off the books
Refuse politely, and tell your supervisor. Side deals cheat the business and leave the customer with no warranty.
A customer will not pay, or disputes the bill
Stay polite, do not argue about money on the spot, and refer it to your supervisor with the facts
A customer's demand is unsafe
Explain the danger, offer the safe option, refuse politely if they insist, and tell your supervisor

blocks.p: Customers in Jamaica are also protected by consumer protection law. A customer who cannot get a complaint settled with a business can take it to the Consumer Affairs Commission, so it is in everyone's interest to settle complaints fairly and quickly.

A short call or message a few days after the job shows the customer that the business cares after it has been paid. It also catches small problems early, such as a gate that needs its hinges adjusted or a light sensor set wrongly, before they turn into complaints.

ul: Call or message at a suitable time, politely: "Good afternoon, Mrs Clarke. It's Omar from the workshop. I'm calling to check the gate is working well for you."
Ask whether everything is working and whether they were happy with the service.
Deal with any problem quickly, and thank them for their time.
Ask for feedback after the job, by a short call, a feedback form or a review. Do not wait for complaints, and do not guess from how much the customer paid.
Record what customers say and pass it to your supervisor: praise as well as problems.
Use feedback to improve: if several customers say the same thing, the business needs to change something.

blocks.p: Accurate records mean the next person can give the right service without asking the customer to repeat everything. Keep customer details, job notes, enquiry forms, quotations, invoices, receipts, warranty details and the complaints log accurate, complete and up to date.

ul: Write clearly, with dates, and spell names correctly.

Keep records **private**: only people who need them may see them. Jamaica's data protection law expects businesses to protect customers' personal information and use it only for the reason it was given.
Never share or sell customers' details, or show them on your phone to others.

Pass on messages and changes **quickly** to the right person, and write them on the job sheet: a customer who changed the size of a grill, materials that will be late, a customer who called to complain.
Then the welder, the electrician or the office can act, and the customer does not have to explain twice.
Tell your supervisor or team what went wrong on a job, so that the cause is fixed for every future customer, not just this one.
Good teamwork means jobs are done right the first time, and on time.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it in a role play with a classmate.

ul: I can explain who external and internal customers are, and give examples from my trade.
I can explain what quality customer service is and why it matters to a business.
I can present myself professionally and make a good first impression.
I can greet customers, and deal with a customer who arrives while I am busy.
I can listen actively and repeat the main points back to check.
I can use open, closed and probing questions.
I can explain trade words in plain language, and use positive body language.
I can answer the phone professionally, put a caller on hold and take an accurate message.
I can find out what a customer needs, explain the options and record the job request.
I can explain a quotation, invoice, receipt and warranty.
I can keep promises, and tell a customer early when something will be late.
I can refuse an unsafe request politely and offer a safe alternative.
I can work in a customer's home or business with care for their property, family and privacy.
I can adapt my service for older customers, customers with disabilities and visitors.
I can handle a complaint step by step and record it in the complaints log.
I can stay calm with an angry customer and keep myself safe.
I can say what I may decide and what I must refer to my supervisor.
I can follow up after a job, collect feedback and keep accurate, private records.
I can pass information on to my team so jobs are done right and on time.

terms: Giving full attention and checking that you have understood
Communication without words: face, eyes, hands and posture; also called non-verbal communication
A small card with your name, the business's name and a phone number
A question answered with yes, no or a short fact, used to confirm a detail
The record of every complaint and what was done about it
Keeping a customer's private information secret
Anyone who receives a product or service from you
How pleased customers are with the service they received
The date or time by which you have promised to finish a job
Someone outside the business who buys from it or uses its service
What a customer decides about you in the first moments of meeting
Contacting the customer after a job to check they are satisfied
An identification badge showing your name and the business
A co-worker who needs your work to do their job
The document asking a customer to pay for work done
Trade or technical words that most customers will not understand
A question that gets the customer talking, which cannot be answered with yes or no
A fixed price for the work, given before the job is agreed
Proof that a customer has paid
A customer who comes back to the business again and again
The level of service a business promises every customer; sometimes a customer charter
A recorded message left on a phone when nobody answers
A written promise that faulty work or parts will be put right free for a set time; also called a guarantee

c1.title: An enquiry at the counter in Savanna-la-Mar
c1.text: Mr Reid, who is about 75 and walks with a stick, comes into a small fabrication shop in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland. He says he wants "something to stop the thieves getting in round the back". There is no seat at the high counter. Romaine, who is serving, knows the shop makes grills from light flat bar and from heavier square bar, at quite different prices.

c2.title: The office phone at an electrical contractor in Half Way Tree
c2.text: Kimberley answers the phone at an electrical contractor's office in Half Way Tree, St Andrew. A caller, Mrs Ellis, is upset: the electrician, Mr Clarke, was booked to come to her house yesterday at 10 a.m. but never arrived and nobody called her. Mr Clarke was sent to an emergency job instead. Kimberley needs to check the job book before she can say when he can come.

c3.title: Rewiring a bakery in Mandeville
c3.text: Lascelles, an electrician, is rewiring a small bakery in Mandeville, Manchester. The owner, Mrs Facey, bakes from 4 a.m. every day and has large orders for Saturday. The power must be off for about five hours. She asks Lascelles to "just add two more sockets on the old circuit" for a new mixer, to save money, although that circuit already trips when the oven and the mixer run together.

c4.title: Rattling burglar bars in Yallahs
c4.text: Mrs Thompson comes into a welding shop in Yallahs, St Thomas, and raises her voice: the burglar bars fitted at her house last week rattle every time the wind blows, and there are paint drips on her new tiles. Kevin is on the counter. He looks at the job sheet and sees that the fitter used fewer fixings than the shop usually does. The shop agrees to send the fitter back on Friday.

c5.title: A gate under warranty in Port Maria
c5.text: Mr Daley's driveway gate was made and fitted four months ago by a shop in Port Maria, St Mary, with a 12-month warranty on workmanship. He calls Omar to say a hinge weld has cracked and the gate drags. He also mentions that his son reversed the car into the gate last month and dented one of the bars.

questions.q: Mr Reid has a walking stick and the counter has no seat. What should Romaine do first?
o: Ask him to come back with someone who can stand with him
Talk to him across the high counter as quickly as possible
Offer him a chair at the desk and talk sitting down
Ask him to phone the shop later from the comfort of home
questions.why: Adapting how you serve someone is part of equal respect. A chair lets Mr Reid take his time and explain properly, and it puts Romaine at his level.

questions.q: How should Romaine explain the two kinds of grill?
o: Show photos of past grills and explain each in plain words, with its price
Describe the bar sizes and weld types in trade terms so he sounds expert
Recommend the dearest grill straight away, because security matters most
Recommend the cheapest grill, since Mr Reid is a pensioner on a fixed income
questions.why: Plain words, pictures and prices let the customer weigh strength against cost and decide for himself. Choosing for him, either way, or hiding behind jargon, is poor service.

questions.q: Mr Reid chooses the heavier grill. What should the written quotation show?
o: The price only, so that the page is simple for him to read
The work, price with GCT shown, validity and finish time
The price, and the name of the welder who will do the job
The work and the price, with the finish date left open for now
questions.why: A quotation sets out what will be done, the price (and whether GCT is included), how long the price holds and when the job will be done, so both sides know what to expect.

questions.q: Kimberley needs to check the job book. How should she put Mrs Ellis on hold?
o: Put the phone down on the desk without saying a word
Ask if she can hold, say how long, and come back
Tell her to call back later when the book is free
Put her on hold and take the next call that comes in
questions.why: Asking first and saying how long shows respect for the caller's time. Come back within that time, or come back to say it will take longer and offer to call her back.

questions.q: What should the business have done yesterday, when it knew Mr Clarke could not go to Mrs Ellis?
o: Waited for Mrs Ellis to call and ask where he was
Sent another worker without telling her who he was
Called her before 10 a.m. to explain and rebook
Called her in the evening once the day's work was done
questions.why: Customers forgive a change of plan far more easily than being left waiting. Telling them before the agreed time, with a reason and a new time, keeps their trust.

questions.q: Kimberley cannot reach Mrs Ellis later and must leave a voicemail. What should it contain?
o: "Call the office", so that Mrs Ellis has to ring back to find out more
A full account of the emergency job that Mr Clarke went to instead
Only the new time, because Mrs Ellis will already know who is calling
Her name, the business, the new time and her number, said slowly
questions.why: A good voicemail says who is calling, from where, why, and how to call back, with the number said slowly so it can be written down. Keep it short and polite.

questions.q: How should Lascelles plan the five-hour power cut?
o: Switch off whenever the team arrives, as the work cannot wait
Agree a time with Mrs Facey that does not stop her baking
Tell her on the morning of the cut so that she is not worried
Leave the power on and work on the live circuits carefully
questions.why: Telling the customer early and agreeing a time that suits the business lets her plan around it. Working on live circuits to avoid a shutdown is never acceptable.

questions.q: How should Lascelles answer the request for two more sockets on the old circuit?
o: Add them, because the customer is paying and has decided
Refuse and say nothing more, since it is against the rules
Add them, but tell her not to use the mixer and oven together
Explain the overload risk simply and price a separate circuit
questions.why: A circuit that already trips is overloaded, and more sockets would make it worse. Explaining the danger in plain words and offering the safe option, with its price, lets her make an informed choice.

questions.q: The rewiring is finished. Which handover is best?
o: Test, clean up, and show her how to reset the new switches
Hand Mrs Facey the invoice and leave before the bakery opens
Leave a note on the board saying the job is done and to call if needed
Ask Mrs Facey to switch everything on herself to see if it works
questions.why: Testing, cleaning up and explaining the new installation in plain words means the customer knows it is safe and what to do if a trip switch goes. Then check she is happy and give the paperwork.

questions.q: Which reply from Kevin shows he understands without arguing?
o: "The wind is very strong in Yallahs, ma'am. That's not our fault."
"Please lower your voice, or I will have to ask you to leave the shop."
"I'm sorry, Mrs Thompson. I can see why you're upset. Tell me more."
"The fitter is not here today, so I can't do anything about it."
questions.why: An apology and a few words showing he understands calm most customers. Blaming the weather, threatening her or passing the problem off makes an angry customer angrier.

questions.q: What should Kevin write in the complaints log?
o: The date, complaint, action agreed, who and by when
Only the customer's name and the single word "rattling"
His opinion of how the customer behaved at the counter
The name of the fitter who caused the whole problem
questions.why: A full record lets anyone see what was promised, by whom and by when, and check it was done. Opinions and blame do not belong in it; the facts and the action do.

questions.q: The fitter fixes the bars on Friday. When and how should the shop follow up?
o: Wait for Mrs Thompson to call back if there is a problem
Send the invoice for the return visit on Monday
Call her a few days later to check all is well
Ask the fitter to tell her he is sorry the next time he passes
questions.why: A call a few days later, after some windy weather, checks that the fix worked and shows the shop cares. It turns a complaint into a satisfied, often loyal, customer.

questions.q: Kevin noticed that the fitter used fewer fixings than usual. What should he do with this?
o: Tell Mrs Thompson that the fitter got it wrong
Keep it to himself to avoid trouble for the fitter
Mention it to the other workers at lunch time
Report it to the supervisor so the method is fixed
questions.why: Passing the cause to the supervisor lets the shop fix its method for every future job, not just this one. Blaming a co-worker in front of a customer looks unprofessional.

questions.q: What should Omar tell Mr Daley about the cracked hinge weld?
o: It is covered, and will be repaired free
It will be repaired, but he must pay for all the labour
The warranty ended on the day his son hit the gate
He must take the gate off and bring it to the shop first
questions.why: A cracked weld four months into a 12-month workmanship warranty is the kind of fault the warranty covers. Honouring it promptly keeps the customer's trust.

questions.q: How should Omar deal with the dented bar?
o: Fix it free and say nothing, to keep Mr Daley happy
Explain that dents are not covered, and offer a quote
Tell Mr Daley the dent caused the crack, so nothing is covered
Refuse to discuss the dent until the hinge has been repaired
questions.why: A warranty covers faulty work, not damage from an accident. Saying so politely, with the warranty terms, and offering a price to repair the dent, is honest and fair.

questions.q: Before he answers, what should Omar check?
o: The weather on the day the gate was fitted
How much Mr Daley paid for the gate
Whether Mr Daley paid in cash or by card
The invoice and warranty terms for the job
questions.why: The invoice shows the date of the job, and the warranty terms show what is covered and for how long. Checking them first means his answer is correct and fair.

questions.q: Heavy traffic means Jason will be about 40 minutes late for a 9 a.m. job. What should he do?
o: Call the customer before 9 a.m. with a new ETA
Arrive late and apologise when he gets there
Text the office and let them tell the customer later
Turn back and book the job for another day
questions.why: A call before the agreed time, with an apology and a realistic new arrival time, lets the customer plan. Arriving late without warning wastes their morning and their trust.

questions.q: Andrea arrives to repair a gate and two large dogs are loose in the yard. What should she do?
o: Go in quickly, as dogs usually settle down
Throw stones near the dogs so that they stay back
Leave and mark the job as cancelled by the customer
Ask the owner to secure the dogs before she goes in
questions.why: Asking the owner to secure pets keeps the worker safe and respects the animals. Keep gates and doors closed behind you while you work so the dogs cannot get out.

questions.q: Shane arrives at the home of an older customer, Miss Gordon, for the first time. Which greeting is best?
o: "Yes, Mommy! I'm here about the grill. Where is it?"
"Good morning, Miss Gordon. I'm Shane, from the workshop."
"Hi, Pauline! I'm from the shop. Where's the grill you want fixed?"
"Morning. Workshop sent me. Show me where the grill is, please."
questions.why: A polite greeting with her title and surname, his own name and the business makes a good first impression. Calling her by her first name or a pet name uninvited, or a curt order, can seem disrespectful to an older customer.

questions.q: A customer offers Dwayne J$5,000 cash "for yourself" if he does a job on Saturday off the books, cheaper than the shop's price. What should he do?
o: Accept, as long as he does the job well
Accept, and give the shop part of the money
Refuse politely, and tell his supervisor
Ask for J$10,000 instead, as it is a weekend
questions.why: Side deals cheat the employer, leave the customer with no warranty or comeback, and can cost the worker his job. Refuse politely and pass the enquiry to the business.
